newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. probes widespread abuses in Rwanda tribunal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. probes widespread abuses in Rwanda tribunal.

text.p: Two years after its creation, the Rwanda war crimes tribunal suffers from mismanagement, unqualified staff and neglect from New York headquarters, according to a new U.N. investigation.

The report, released on Wednesday, sets out in detail financial abuses and mismangement in the administrative apparatus as well as apparent legal chaos in the prosecutor's office set up to investigate the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

Some of the complaints emerged several months ago and both Secretary-General Kofi Annan and his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali have made key personnel changes. But the report called for further "substantial" changes.

Otherwise "the Rwandese will be right to suspect that justice delayed is justice denied," said the report by Karl Paschke, the U.N.'s equivalent of an inspector-general, who heads the Office of Internal Oversight Services.

Annan "was struck by the breadth of the criticism of the administration of the Rwanda tribunal," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said. "We owe it to the half million victims of genocide in Rwanda to do better than we have done."
Annan will take further action after a meeting he has called for Feb. 21 with Prosecutor Louise Arbor, Deputy Prosecutor Honoure Rakotomanana and Registrar Andronico Adede, Eckhard said.

Paschke in his report recommended replacing the deputy prosecutor but in answer to questions said he did not recommend the same for Adede because of the complex situation he was facing. Most of the criticism in the report was directed at Adede, a former legal affairs officer in New York.

Set up in Arusha, Tanzania, the tribunal is to try leaders responsible for more than half a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus massacred in Rwanda in 1994 by Hutu troops and others. A sub-office for prosecutors and investigators is located in the Rwandan capital of Kigali. Paschke said the split in locations had contributed to mistrust and misunderstandings.

In the Arusha registrar's office headed by Adede, Pashke said, "not a single administrative area" functioned effectively. There was no accounting system, budgets were haphazard and staff in key jobs were unqualified.

One employee received a double salary, kept silent about it, asked for an advance and still owes the United Nations more than $34,000. Yet his contract was extended until mid-1997, with the approval of the personnel department.

In another instance a plane costing $27,000 went to pick up suspects in Cameroon but left empty because of no prior agreement with that country for surrendering the prisoners. Cameroon in January finally did hand over four suspects including Col. Theoneste Bagosora, described as giving military orders at the beginning of the 1994 massacres.

The tribunal has indicted 21 people. The first trial is under way against Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, the former mayor of Rwanda's Taba commune, charged with inciting the public to slaughter and ordering killings.

Paschke said the prosecutor's office in Kigali suffered from inexperienced staff and a lack of vehicles, computers and office equipment. The prosecutor -- first Richard Goldstone of South Africa, now Arbor of Canada -- is chief prosecutor for the Hague-based tribunal on the former Yugoslavia also.
Goldstone's instructions to concentrate indictments on national figures first were ignored and various legal staff followed their own strategies at will, the report said.

Paschke said many tasks had to be performed without support or resources from New York, particularly the departments of legal affairs, headed by Hans Corell of Sweden, and administration and management, headed by Joseph Connor of the United States.

"The evidence suggests that once a few key administrators were selected the secretariat failed to take responsibiity to provide essential support for the tribunal until it could become functional," he said.
